header.competitor: Unnamed competitor (never named in the interview)
header.incumbent: Unnamed existing payments provider whose support was a ticket form
header.tag_why: The COO decided on who picks up during an on-sale. The competitor showed named people and promised on-sale on-call coverage, while we answered "who's my person" with support tiers she called "a queue with a faster timer."

messaging_changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
messaging_changes.change: For operational buyers (COO, ops leads) at merchants whose revenue comes in spikes, such as on-sales: "A name, not a queue." Lead with the named people the customer will have, such as a solutions engineer and an account lead, and the escalation path they call during a live failure. Do not lead with tiers or response times. Only name coverage commitments our solutions engineering team has confirmed we can staff.
messaging_changes.why: When the decider asked "who's my person" and got the support plans, she called them "a queue with a faster timer", so the tiered-response framing described the ticket-form problem she was trying to escape.

messaging_changes.change: For merchants with scheduled peak events: add an "on-sale morning" coverage plan as a proof asset. It should show, on paper, who is watching, who the customer calls, and what we do in the first minutes after payments start failing. Build it with our solutions engineer for each deal until it exists as a standard offering, and include only commitments we have confirmed internally.
messaging_changes.why: The decider wanted to see on paper what we do on an on-sale morning, and the rep said "We don't have that as a thing" even though he could have built it with our solutions engineer.

messaging_changes.change: Opening line for operational buyers at spike-driven merchants, used in place of the global-growth opener and uptime statistics: frame the pitch around what happens in the first minutes of a live failure, in the customer's words: "I don't buy uptime, I buy what happens when it's down." Make this pitch directly to the operational decider, not through the technical champion.
messaging_changes.why: The deal was triggered by a live failure where support replied only after the on-sale was over, and the decider who made the call in one meeting rejected uptime as the thing she buys while our technical proof reached her only secondhand.

messaging_changes.change: Proof point alongside customer stories for operational buyers: offer a reference person who can describe how we responded during a live spike or incident, not just a logo.
messaging_changes.why: The rep said "I had logos. I didn't have a person." to a buyer whose test was "A name, not a queue."

trigger.insight: Payments failing was not new: per Ben it had happened twice before and nobody switched. What changed was that the CEO saw it in public and the provider's ticket form replied only after the on-sale had ended. This evaluation started as an incident-response problem owned by the COO, not a platform-performance problem owned by the CTO, and the deal was framed that way from the first Monday.
trigger.messaging: For ticketing and other spike-driven merchants, open with what happens in the first minutes of a live failure during an on-sale, not with M1's global-growth positioning.

competitor.insight: Everything we know about the competitor comes through Ben, and none of it is product. They won on people who were present and on a coverage promise tied to the customer's own calendar of on-sales. That meeting reset the evaluation criteria from throughput to names. The rep's theory that they over-promised is unverified by his own admission, and even if it is true, an over-promise beat our accurate answer because ours did not answer the question. The competitor's name, and whether Halima attended that meeting, were never established.
competitor.messaging: Don't counter with doubt about whether competitors can staff every event. Make our own concrete commitment instead: named people plus defined coverage for the customer's major events.

message.insight: The developer and technical story (M2, the sandbox, uptime, the bot and fraud tooling) landed with the people who did not decide. The decider gave it one word. M5's framing of tiered response times is, in Halima's words, a queue with a faster timer. That is exactly what the incumbent's ticket form was, just faster, so our support message described the problem she was trying to escape.
message.messaging: Rewrite M5 away from tiers and response times toward named people, an escalation path and event coverage, because response-time language reads as the same queue the customer is fleeing.

decided.insight: The rep's sense that we were the favourite rested on the champion's confidence, not on the decider's. Ben planning the integration shows that the CTO was sold, which was never the question. The loss became visible at Halima's remark, but the opening was there earlier: she asked who, and we answered with a plan sheet.
decided.messaging: Treat a decider's who question as the moment that decides the deal, and give the answer in names and a minute-by-minute plan, never in a tier table.

gaps.insight: There were two gaps, and only one is a product gap. We have no packaged event or on-sale plan. A plan could have been assembled with our solutions engineer, so the deal was lost partly on execution, not capability. On the proof side, M8's customer stories and logos do not answer who picked up; this buyer needed a reference person who had lived through a live incident with us.
gaps.messaging: Create a peak-event coverage plan asset (who's watching, who you call, what happens at minute four) and a reference program that offers a person who can describe our response during a live spike, not just a logo.

language.insight: The customer's vocabulary is about people and moments, not service categories: "who," "a name," "someone who picks up," "on-sale morning." Halima's uptime line directly rejects the reliability-statistics framing we led with. Our words (support, tiers, uptime) are the categories she has said she is not buying.
language.messaging: Adopt the customer's framing in peak-event messaging, for example "a name, not a queue" and "what happens when it's down," and drop uptime history as the lead proof point for operational buyers.

gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan to check with Ben after the spring on-sales whether the promised shared channel and on-call coverage were delivered.

gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan, or Ben, who from Tixhaven attended that meeting.

gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan and our solutions engineer what we could have committed to, and whether anyone was asked.

gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan whether pricing or terms came up in the final meeting, per Ben.

gaps.question: Does Ben still believe we were the better platform?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Jordan to confirm directly with Ben rather than assume.

close.rep_takeaway: Your champion being sold is not the same as the decider being sold. When the person who decides asks "who's my person," answer with a name and a plan for their worst morning, built with your solutions engineer if needed, not a tier sheet. Halima told you what she buys: what happens when it's down.
